Food safety standards for all food products
Right to free meals for all citizens
explanation: National Food Security Act 2013 provides legal entitlement to subsidised food grains (5 kg per person per month at Rs. 1-3/kg) to up to 75% of rural population and 50% of urban population. Also covers pregnant women, lactating mothers, and children under 14 years.

question: The Persons with Disabilities Act 1995 was replaced by which legislation?
options: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016
explanation: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 replaced the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act 1995. The 2016 Act aligns Indian law with CRPD 2006, increases specified disabilities from 7 to 21, mandates 5% reservation.

question: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 operationalises which constitutional provision?
options: Article 21A - Right to Education (86th Constitutional Amendment)
explanation: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act 2002, making free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6-14 years. The RTE Act 2009 gives legislative effect to Article 21A. It mandates 25% reservation for EWS in private unaided schools.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 defines 'human rights' to mean rights relating to:
options: Only rights enumerated in the Constitution of India
Life, liberty, equality and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in International Covenants and enforceable by courts in India
Rights under ICCPR and ICESCR only
explanation: Section 2(1)(d) of the PHR Act 1993: 'Human rights' means the rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity of the individual guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in the International Covenants and enforceable by courts in India.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The State Human Rights Commission under the PHR Act 1993 can inquire into:
options: Any human rights violation by anyone
Complaints of violations of human rights only in respect of matters relatable to entries in List II and List III of the Seventh Schedule
Violations relating to armed forces in the state
explanation: Section 29 of PHR Act 1993: The State Human Rights Commission may inquire into complaints of violations in respect of matters relatable to any of the entries in List II (State List) and List III (Concurrent List). It cannot inquire into matters under List I (Union List).

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: Under the PHR Act 1993, the NHRC consists of:
options: Chairperson and not more than 5 members (after 2019 amendment)
Chairperson, 3 judicial members and 2 expert members
explanation: The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act 2019 amended the composition: NHRC consists of a Chairperson (retired CJI or SC judge) and not more than 5 members. Ex-officio members include Chairpersons of NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW, and NCBC.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The National Commission for Women Act 1990 empowers the NCW to:
options: Review constitutional and legal safeguards, take up cases of violations, and make recommendations for remedial legislation
Prosecute offenders directly in criminal courts
Appoint special public prosecutors in all women-related cases
explanation: Under the NCW Act 1990, the NCW's functions include: reviewing constitutional and legal safeguards for women; recommending remedial legislative measures; facilitating redressal of grievances; and advising the Central Government on policies affecting women.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 established which specialized courts?
options: Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts
explanation: The SC/ST (POA) Act 1989 provides for: Special Courts (designated Sessions Courts) for trial of offences under the Act; and after the 2015 Amendment, Exclusive Special Courts (dedicated courts dealing exclusively with atrocity cases) in districts with higher incidence. A Special Public Prosecutor must be appointed.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 was enacted to:
options: Protect civil rights of all citizens
Give effect to Article 17 - abolition of untouchability - and prescribe punishment for practising untouchability
explanation: The Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955) gives effect to Article 17 of the Constitution which abolishes untouchability. It prescribes punishment for enforcing disabilities arising from untouchability.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The National Commission for Backward Classes Act 1993 provided for examination of complaints relating to:
options: Inclusion in and exclusion from the lists of backward classes and conditions of backwardness
explanation: Under the NCBC Act 1993, the Commission examined requests for inclusion of communities in central lists of backward classes and complaints of over-inclusion or under-inclusion. After the 102nd Constitutional Amendment 2018, the power to identify SEBCs for central purposes vests with the President on Commission's advice.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The NHRC cannot inquire into a matter if it is already pending before:
options: A State Human Rights Commission or any other Commission constituted under any law
explanation: Section 36(1) of PHR Act 1993: The Commission shall not inquire into any matter which is pending before a State Commission or any other Commission duly constituted under any law for the time being in force. This prevents overlapping jurisdiction between NHRC and SHRCs or specialized commissions.

question: Which of the following accurately describes the relationship between environmental rights and human rights?
options: A clean and healthy environment is increasingly recognized as a prerequisite for the enjoyment of human rights, particularly right to life
They are entirely separate and independent streams of law
Human rights law takes precedence over environmental law in all cases
Environmental rights can only be claimed by citizens, not non-citizens
explanation: The relationship between environmental rights and human rights is one of mutual reinforcement. UNHRC Resolution 48/13 (2021) and UNGA Resolution 76/300 (2022) recognized the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a human right. Indian SC has long held environmental degradation violates Article 21.

question: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the right to education is a fundamental right under Article 21?
options: Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992)
TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002)
P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005)
Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)
explanation: Unni Krishnan v. State of AP (1993) - the SC held that the right to education is a fundamental right flowing from Article 21 for children up to 14 years. This was subsequently given explicit constitutional basis through Article 21A by the 86th Amendment 2002.

question: The doctrine of 'proportionality' in human rights law means:
options: Equal compensation for all human rights violations
Proportional representation of minorities in Parliament
Equal application of rights to all communities
Any restriction on human rights must be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and must not go beyond what is necessary
explanation: Proportionality is a fundamental principle of human rights law - restrictions on rights must be: (i) prescribed by law; (ii) in pursuit of a legitimate aim; (iii) necessary in a democratic society; and (iv) proportionate to the aim. The SC has increasingly applied proportionality analysis in Indian constitutional law.

question: The 'phrase rarest of rare' in Indian law relates to:
options: Cancellation of bail in heinous offences
Imposition of death penalty - evolved in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980)
explanation: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) - the SC upheld the constitutional validity of the death penalty but laid down the 'rarest of rare' doctrine: death sentence should be imposed only when the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.

question: The Right to Information Act 2005 is relevant to environmental law because:
options: It only applies to income tax and administrative matters
It allows citizens to obtain environmental data, pollution records, EIA reports, and inspection reports from public authorities
It exempts all environmental information from disclosure
It applies only to Central Government departments
explanation: RTI Act 2005 is a powerful tool for environmental democracy - citizens can seek: pollution monitoring data from PCBs; EIA reports and environmental clearances from MoEFCC; inspection reports of industries. Section 8(2) mandates disclosure of environmental information even relating to trade secrets if public interest outweighs the harm.

question: The Directive Principles of State Policy relating to environmental protection are:
options: Non-justiciable but fundamental to governance, and courts have read them with Art 21 to create enforceable environmental rights
Justiciable and can be directly enforced by courts
Superior to Fundamental Rights in all cases
Applicable only to the Central Government
explanation: DPSPs (including Art 48A on environment) are non-justiciable under Article 37 - but the SC has consistently used them to expand the scope of Article 21. Article 48A has been read with Article 21 to create a judicially enforceable right to clean environment through harmonious construction.

question: The term 'environment' in its legal sense was first defined in Indian law under:
explanation: The first comprehensive statutory definition of 'environment' in Indian law appears in Section 2(a) of the Environment Protection Act 1986. Earlier legislations like the Water Act 1974 and Air Act 1981 dealt with specific media but did not define 'environment' as a whole.

question: The 'neighbour principle' in environmental liability originated from:
options: Cambridge Water Co. v. Eastern Counties Leather, 1994
explanation: The neighbour principle from Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932 - Lord Atkin) - you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would likely injure your neighbour - is the foundational principle of negligence liability applied in tort-based environmental compensation claims.

question: 'Ecocentrism' differs from 'anthropocentrism' in environmental law in that:
options: Ecocentrism places human interests at the centre of environmental decision-making
Anthropocentrism prohibits all human use of natural resources
They are essentially the same concept with different names
Ecocentrism treats the entire ecosystem as having intrinsic value, not merely instrumental value for humans
explanation: Anthropocentrism (human-centred) protects environment for human benefit. Ecocentrism (ecosystem-centred) treats ecosystems, species, and nature as having intrinsic worth independent of human use. The Rights of Nature movement (Ecuador's constitution, 2008) reflects ecocentrism.

question: In which case did the Supreme Court apply the doctrine of 'sustainable development' to order balance between environment and development?
options: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (Forest case, 1995 - ongoing)
Rural Litigation Kendra v. State of UP (1985)
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991)
explanation: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. UOI (1995 onwards) - the landmark ongoing Forest case in which the SC has been monitoring forest protection across India. The court applied sustainable development to hold that while development is necessary, it cannot destroy forests; non-forest use requires prior Central Government approval.

question: The concept of 'joint and several liability' in environmental law means:
options: All polluters are equally liable regardless of their contribution
Each polluter can be held fully liable for the total environmental damage even if multiple parties contributed
Liability is divided proportionally among all polluters
Only the largest polluter bears the full liability
explanation: Joint and several liability means each liable party can be held responsible for the full amount of environmental damage, regardless of their proportionate contribution. This is significant in cases of multiple polluters - the victim does not have to sue each polluter separately for their share.

question: 'Biopiracy' in the context of environmental and IPR law refers to:
options: Illegal hunting and poaching of wildlife
Unauthorized appropriation of biological resources and traditional knowledge of indigenous communities by commercial entities without fair compensation
explanation: Biopiracy - the appropriation of traditional biological resources and associated knowledge (of tribal/indigenous communities) by corporations, often through patents, without consent or benefit-sharing. The Neem patent controversy, Turmeric patent, and Basmati case are classic Indian examples. Addressed by Nagoya Protocol 2010 and Biological Diversity Act 2002.

question: The term 'environmental refugee' refers to:
options: A person who has committed environmental crimes and fled the country
A refugee who is granted asylum on environmental grounds
A person displaced from their usual place of residence due to environmental disruption - rising seas, drought, floods etc.
A person who voluntarily migrates to environmentally pristine areas
explanation: Environmental/climate refugees are persons displaced by environmental changes - rising sea levels, desertification, floods, droughts. They are not recognized under the 1951 Refugee Convention (which covers only persecution-based displacement). This is an evolving area of international law.

question: The 'no harm' rule in international environmental law means:
options: States must not cause any environmental harm within their territory
No state can harm the global commons
A state must not allow activities within its territory to cause significant transboundary environmental harm to other states
Nuclear testing is prohibited in all circumstances
explanation: The 'no harm' principle - originating in the Trail Smelter Arbitration (USA v. Canada, 1938-41) - holds that no state has the right to use or permit use of its territory in such a manner as to cause injury to the territory of another state. Codified in Stockholm Principle 21 and Rio Principle 2.

question: The Trail Smelter Arbitration (1941) is significant because:
options: It was the first international adjudication holding a state responsible for transboundary air pollution
It established the principle of common heritage of mankind
It created the first international environmental court
explanation: Trail Smelter Case (USA v. Canada, 1941) - fumes from a Canadian smelter caused damage to crops and forests in Washington state, USA. The arbitral tribunal held Canada responsible and directed cessation of harmful emissions. This is the foundational case for state responsibility for transboundary environmental harm.

question: The Gabcikovo-Nagymaros Project case (Hungary v. Slovakia, ICJ 1997) dealt with:
options: Nuclear waste in the Danube River
Oil pollution of the Black Sea
Suspension of a joint dam project on the Danube - ICJ applied sustainable development and EIA principles
explanation: Gabcikovo-Nagymaros (1997) - Hungary unilaterally suspended a joint dam project with Slovakia citing environmental concerns. ICJ held both parties had violated treaty obligations and notably applied the principle of sustainable development and recognized evolving environmental norms.

question: The 'Polluter Pays Principle' in the Rio Declaration is contained in:
explanation: Rio Declaration Principle 16: National authorities should endeavour to promote the internalization of environmental costs, taking into account the approach that the polluter should, in principle, bear the cost of pollution. Principle 15 = Precautionary; Principle 7 = CBDR; Principle 10 = Access to information.

question: The Kyoto Protocol's 'Clean Development Mechanism' (CDM) allows:
options: Developed countries to buy emission credits from projects in developing countries
Developing countries to impose emission caps on developed countries
Countries to avoid emission reductions by paying a fine
Carbon trading among developing countries only
explanation: CDM under the Kyoto Protocol (Article 12): Allows developed countries (Annex I parties) to implement emission-reduction projects in developing countries and earn Certified Emission Reduction (CER) credits, allowing them to partially meet their Kyoto targets.

question: The concept of 'environmental constitutionalism' refers to:
options: Environmental laws enacted by Parliament only
Constitutional review of all environmental legislation
Inclusion of environmental rights and duties in national constitutions
explanation: Environmental constitutionalism - the incorporation of environmental rights, duties or principles in national constitutions. India (Articles 48A and 51A(g)), Ecuador (Rights of Nature), South Africa (Section 24 - right to environment) are leading examples. Over 150 countries now have some form of constitutional environmental provision.

question: The Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Ganga Pollution case) directed:
options: Closure of all industries near River Ganga
Tanneries and other polluting industries discharging into the Ganga to set up effluent treatment plants or face closure
Construction of a dam to control Ganga flooding
explanation: M.C. Mehta v. UOI (Ganga Pollution cases, 1987-88 onwards) - a series of orders directing tanneries, municipalities, and industries discharging untreated effluents into the River Ganga to install effluent treatment plants (ETPs) or face closure.

question: The concept of 'extended producer responsibility' (EPR) in waste management means:
options: Producers are responsible for the entire lifecycle of their products including post-consumer waste management
Producers are responsible only for the quality of their products
Responsibility of large producers to support small producers
Government's extended responsibility for industrial waste
explanation: EPR - manufacturers/importers/brand owners are responsible for their products' environmental impact throughout the product lifecycle, including collection, recycling or disposal of post-consumer waste. EPR is incorporated in India's E-Waste Rules, Plastic Waste Management Rules, and Battery Waste Management Rules under EPA 1986.

question: Under the Forest Conservation Act 1980, 'non-forest purpose' explicitly excludes:
options: Reforestation or afforestation - which is considered a forest purpose
explanation: Forest Conservation Act 1980, Section 2 Explanation: 'Non-forest purpose' does not include reforestation or afforestation. Planting trees on forest land is a forest purpose and does not require Central Government approval.

question: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers Act 2006 vests rights in forest dwellers as of:
options: Date of enactment of the Act
13 December 2005 - the cut-off date for establishing occupation
Date of grant of patta by State Government
explanation: The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognizes rights of those who have been occupying forest land for cultivation or habitation as of 13 December 2005 (the cut-off date). The individual has to prove occupation through at least two of the three specified periods. This cut-off date is the most commonly tested factual detail from this Act.

question: The Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification 2019 classifies coastal areas into how many categories?
explanation: CRZ Notification 2019 classifies coastal areas into 4 zones: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive, intertidal zone - most restricted); CRZ-II (urban areas); CRZ-III (rural coastal areas, divided into III-A and III-B); CRZ-IV (water area up to 12 nautical miles including islands). This replaced the CRZ Notification 2011.

question: The 'Doctrine of Public Trust' applies in India to which categories of resources?
options: Only rivers and seas - not forests
Air, sea, water, forests and other natural resources held by the State in trust for the public
Only resources specifically enumerated in the Environment Protection Act
explanation: As articulated in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) and subsequent cases, the Public Trust Doctrine in India applies to air, sea, water, forests, seashores, and natural resources generally - held by the State in trust for the public and cannot be alienated for private commercial purposes.

question: The NGT in Almitra H. Patel v. Union of India dealt with:
options: Solid waste management and garbage dumping in cities
explanation: Almitra H. Patel v. UOI is the landmark case on municipal solid waste management in India. The SC/NGT issued extensive directions for implementation of Municipal Solid Waste Rules and subsequently Solid Waste Management Rules 2016.

question: Which of the following matters falls WITHIN the NGT's jurisdiction under Schedule I of the NGT Act 2010?
options: Matters under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974
Matters under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972
Matters under the Biological Diversity Act 2002 (excluded from Schedule I)
explanation: Schedule I of the NGT Act 2010 lists environmental laws within NGT's jurisdiction including: Water Act 1974, Water Cess Act 1977, Air Act 1981, EPA 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991. The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 is excluded from Schedule I.

question: The Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 was enacted to:
options: Provide mandatory insurance for immediate relief to victims of accidents involving hazardous substances, on a no-fault basis
Provide insurance to public sector undertakings
Create a government fund for environmental disasters
Provide life insurance for workers in hazardous industries
explanation: Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 requires every owner handling hazardous substances to take out an insurance policy to meet liability for giving immediate relief to victims of accidents. Relief is on a no-fault basis. The Act was a legislative response to the Bhopal Gas Tragedy.

question: The 'social contract' theory of rights as developed by Rousseau differs from Locke's theory in that:
options: Rousseau rejected all notion of natural rights
Rousseau located sovereignty in the 'general will' of the community rather than in individual natural rights
Rousseau's theory applies only to economic rights
explanation: Locke's social contract preserves pre-existing natural rights (life, liberty, property) against the state. Rousseau's General Will (volonte generale) locates authority in the collective will of the community - the individual gives up natural freedom for civil freedom within the community.

question: Jeremy Bentham's criticism of natural rights was that:
options: Natural rights are 'nonsense upon stilts' - they are fictional claims that have no objective basis
Rights are too difficult to enforce
Rights should be granted only to wealthy citizens
Natural rights conflict with state sovereignty
explanation: Bentham famously called natural rights 'nonsense upon stilts' - arguing that rights can only exist as positive legal rights created and enforced by the state; natural rights without legal backing are merely rhetorical assertions.

question: The 'Rawlsian veil of ignorance' thought experiment is designed to:
options: Show that people are naturally selfish
Derive principles of justice that would be chosen by rational persons without knowledge of their place in society
Argue for equal distribution of all resources
explanation: In Rawls' 'Theory of Justice' (1971): behind the 'veil of ignorance' (not knowing your gender, race, class, talents), rational persons would choose: (1) equal basic liberties for all; (2) inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged (difference principle).

question: Ronald Dworkin's concept of rights as 'trumps' means:
options: Rights always override each other in a fixed hierarchy
Strong rights belong only to citizens
Individual rights function as constraints on utilitarian calculations - they cannot be overridden merely because doing so would produce greater aggregate welfare
Rights of the majority always prevail
explanation: Ronald Dworkin (Taking Rights Seriously, 1977): Rights are 'trumps' that individuals can play against the state - even when overriding them would benefit society overall. This is an anti-utilitarian conception of rights setting side-constraints on what majorities or governments can do to individuals.

question: The 'Responsibility to Protect' (R2P) doctrine holds that:
options: When a state fails to protect its population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, the international community has a responsibility to intervene
States are responsible for protecting their own citizens only
Responsibility to protect applies only to economic rights
Only the UN Security Council bears responsibility to protect citizens worldwide
explanation: R2P was developed by the International Commission on Intervention and State Sovereignty (ICISS) in 2001 and endorsed at the 2005 UN World Summit. When states fail to protect their populations, the international community (through the Security Council) has a residual responsibility.

question: The 'erga omnes' concept in human rights law means:
options: Obligations owed by states to the international community as a whole - all states have a legal interest in their fulfillment
Rights enforceable only against the state that violates them
Rights enforceable only by regional human rights courts
Obligations of individuals toward the state
explanation: Erga omnes (towards all) obligations - recognized by ICJ in Barcelona Traction case (1970) - are obligations a state owes to the entire international community. Core human rights obligations (prohibition of genocide, slavery, racial discrimination, torture) are erga omnes - any state may invoke responsibility for their breach.

question: The concept of 'positive obligations' in human rights law means:
options: States must take active steps to ensure rights are realized - including legislation, administrative measures, and provision of resources
States only have to refrain from violating rights
Obligations that are positively worded in treaties
Obligations with which states have voluntarily agreed to comply
explanation: Positive obligations go beyond negative duties (not to torture, not to arbitrarily detain) - states must actively ensure rights through legislation, judicial systems, police protection, social services, and resource allocation. Even ICCPR rights impose positive obligations (e.g., right to fair trial requiring courts and legal aid).

question: The 'Lotus Principle' in international law states:
options: States must always seek permission before acting internationally
States must protect their territory's environment
States can only act where explicitly authorized by international law
Everything not prohibited in international law is permitted to sovereign states
explanation: The Lotus Principle (PCIJ, S.S. Lotus case, 1927): States are free to act unless international law expressly prohibits them. This principle has environmental law implications - it was used historically to argue that states could pollute unless specifically prohibited. Modern environmental law has increasingly constrained this through the no-harm rule and precautionary principle.

question: The 'travaux preparatoires' of the UDHR show that the drafting committee included:
options: Only Western nations drafted the UDHR
All 58 UN member states at the time actively participated in drafting
The drafting committee had diverse representation - China, Lebanon, France, USA among others including India's Hansa Mehta
explanation: The UDHR drafting committee had diverse membership including: Eleanor Roosevelt (USA), Rene Cassin (France), Peng Chun Chang (China), Charles Malik (Lebanon), Hansa Mehta (India - who ensured 'all human beings' instead of 'all men'). This diversity counters the claim that UDHR is purely a Western document.

question: Under the ICCPR, the right to life (Article 6) is interpreted to impose on states:
options: Only negative obligation not to take life arbitrarily
Both negative (not to kill arbitrarily) and positive (to take measures to protect life against threats including environmental hazards) obligations
Only obligation to abolish the death penalty
explanation: The Human Rights Committee's General Comment 36 on Article 6 (2018) gave the right to life its broadest interpretation: states must not arbitrarily deprive of life AND must take positive measures to protect life - including against threats from private actors, environmental degradation, climate change, and industrial pollution.

question: A 'Covenant' was chosen as the form for ICCPR and ICESCR (rather than a declaration) because:
options: A Covenant is a legally binding treaty - unlike a declaration, it creates binding obligations on ratifying states
Declarations are not recognized in international law
Declarations cannot be adopted by the General Assembly
The term Covenant has religious significance appropriate for rights instruments
explanation: Both ICCPR and ICESCR are in the form of international treaties (Covenants) that create binding legal obligations on state parties who ratify them. The UDHR is a declaration - a statement of aspirations. Choosing the Covenant form gave the rights legally enforceable character with monitoring mechanisms.

question: Which of the following is a non-treaty-based (Charter-based) human rights body?
options: Committee on the Rights of the Child
explanation: The UN Human Rights Council is a Charter-based body - it derives its authority from the UN Charter, not from a specific human rights treaty. Treaty-based bodies (Human Rights Committee, CESCR, CEDAW Committee etc.) derive their authority from their respective treaties.

question: The principle of 'best interests of the child' under the CRC applies to:
options: All actions concerning children whether by public or private social welfare institutions, courts, administrative authorities or legislative bodies
explanation: CRC Article 3(1): In all actions concerning children, whether undertaken by public or private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities or legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration. 'All actions' is comprehensive.

question: CEDAW defines discrimination against women as:
options: Only intentional acts of discrimination by public authorities
Any distinction, exclusion or restriction made on the basis of sex which results in impairing the exercise of human rights by women in any field
Discrimination only in employment and education
Any act that injures women physically
explanation: CEDAW Article 1: 'Discrimination against women' means any distinction, exclusion or restriction made on the basis of sex which has the effect or purpose of impairing or nullifying the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by women of human rights. The 'effect or purpose' formulation covers both intentional and unintentional discrimination.

question: The 'social model of disability' (which the CRPD 2006 is based on) holds that:
options: Disability is a medical condition that needs to be cured
Disabled persons need charity and welfare, not rights
Disability is a natural condition requiring no special legal framework
Disability results from the interaction between persons with impairments and attitudinal and environmental barriers that hinder their full participation in society
explanation: The social model of disability shifts the focus from the individual's impairment (medical model) to the societal barriers that disable people with impairments. CRPD 2006 is squarely based on the social model - it requires removing barriers and making society inclusive.

question: The Right to Education Act 2009 mandates that private unaided schools must reserve what percentage of seats for economically weaker sections (EWS)?
explanation: Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act 2009: Every private unaided school shall admit in Class I to the extent of at least 25% of the strength of that class, children belonging to the weaker section and disadvantaged group in the neighbourhood. The State Government reimburses these schools for EWS students.

question: The UN Principles for Older Persons (1991) cover which areas?
options: Independence, participation, care, self-fulfillment, and dignity
Rights only in residential care facilities
Economic rights of elderly persons only
explanation: The UN Principles for Older Persons 1991 (UNGA Resolution 46/91) - while non-binding - covers five areas: independence; participation; care; self-fulfillment; and dignity. There is no binding treaty specifically on older persons' rights.

question: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015 defines 'child in conflict with law' as:
options: Any child who is involved in criminal activity regardless of age
Only children below 14 years who commit offences
Children between 16-18 years who commit heinous offences
A child who is alleged or found to have committed an offence and who has not completed 18 years of age on the date of commission of such offence
explanation: JJ Act 2015, Section 2(13): 'Child in conflict with law' means a child who is alleged or found to have committed an offence and who has not completed eighteen years of age on the date of commission of such offence. The special provision for 16-18 year olds in heinous offences is a sub-category.

question: The Women's Reservation Bill (Constitution 106th Amendment Act, 2023) provides for reservation of seats for women in:
options: Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies (and Delhi Assembly)
Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and all State Legislatures
explanation: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) inserts Articles 330A and 332A to reserve one-third of seats for women in Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies (and NCT of Delhi). Reservation will be effective after delimitation following the next Census.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act 2019 made which significant change regarding ex-officio members of NHRC?
options: Replaced ex-officio members with government nominees
Added Chairperson of National Commission for Backward Classes as an ex-officio member
Made ex-officio membership mandatory for CBI Director
explanation: The 2019 Amendment to PHR Act 1993 added the Chairperson of the National Commission for Backward Classes as an ex-officio member of the NHRC. Other ex-officio members remain: Chairpersons of NCM, NCSC, NCST, and NCW.

question: The 'capability approach' developed by Amartya Sen focuses on:
options: Economic capabilities of states to implement human rights
Military capabilities of states to enforce rights
What people are actually able to do and be - their real freedoms and substantive opportunities
Institutional capabilities of national human rights commissions
explanation: Sen's Capability Approach (Development as Freedom, 1999): Human development should be assessed in terms of what individuals are substantively able to do and be (capabilities/freedoms), not merely formal legal rights or income. Martha Nussbaum extended it with a list of 10 central capabilities.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: Section 12 of the PHR Act 1993 specifies the functions of the NHRC. Which of the following is NOT a function of the NHRC?
options: Inquiring into complaints of human rights violations
Reviewing constitutional and legal safeguards for human rights
Directly prosecuting persons who commit human rights violations
Spreading human rights literacy among the masses
explanation: The NHRC does not have the power to directly prosecute - it can recommend prosecution (Section 18) to the concerned government. Its functions include: inquiry into complaints; reviewing safeguards; promoting research and education in human rights; visiting institutions where persons are detained.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The 'Special Rapporteur' system under the UN Human Rights Council is:
options: A Charter-based mechanism - independent experts appointed to examine, monitor, report and advise on human rights situations
An enforcement mechanism with binding powers
Part of the Universal Periodic Review process
explanation: Special Rapporteurs are Charter-based (not treaty-based) - they do not require state ratification to function. They are independent experts appointed by the Human Rights Council to examine specific country situations or thematic issues (torture, violence against women, right to food, right to a clean environment).

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The 'Paris Principles' (1991) relate to:
options: Principles relating to the status and functioning of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights
explanation: The Paris Principles were adopted at the First International Workshop of National Institutions for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights (Paris, 1991) and endorsed by UNGA Resolution 48/134 (1993). They set minimum standards for national human rights institutions (NHRIs) including independence, broad mandate, composition.

topic: Protection & Enforcement of HR in India
question: The appointment of the NHRC Chairperson and Members is made by the:
options: President of India on the recommendation of a Committee headed by the Prime Minister
explanation: Section 4 of the PHR Act 1993: The Chairperson and Members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a Committee consisting of: the Prime Minister (Chairperson of Committee); Speaker of Lok Sabha; Home Minister; Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha; Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha; and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

question: The concept of 'environmental justice' includes:
options: Justice for environmental damage to wildlife only
Compensation payable by states for transboundary pollution
Equitable distribution of environmental benefits and burdens, particularly for marginalized communities, along with procedural access to information and courts
explanation: Environmental justice combines: distributive justice (fair distribution of environmental benefits and burdens); procedural justice (access to information, participation and courts); and corrective justice (remediation and compensation). It connects environmental law to human rights and social justice.

question: Which of the following cases established that the right to shelter/housing is part of Article 21?
options: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)
Chameli Singh v. State of UP (1996)
Francis Coralie Mullin v. UT of Delhi (1981)
explanation: All three cases recognized housing/shelter as part of Article 21: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) - right to live with human dignity includes shelter; Olga Tellis (1985) - right to livelihood and shelter of pavement dwellers; Chameli Singh (1996) - SC explicitly held right to shelter is a fundamental right under Article 21.

question: 'Human rights due diligence' as applied to corporations means:
options: Ongoing process to identify, prevent, mitigate and account for human rights impacts in business operations and value chains
Compliance with domestic labour laws only
Annual reporting on corporate social responsibility
Compensation for environmental damage caused by industrial operations
explanation: Human rights due diligence (under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights 2011 - the Ruggie Framework) requires corporations to: assess actual and potential human rights impacts; integrate findings into business processes; track responses; and communicate how impacts are addressed.

question: The principle that 'human rights are inalienable' means:
options: Rights cannot be transferred to another person or surrendered voluntarily
Rights can never be restricted under any circumstances
Rights belong only to nationals, not aliens
Rights cannot be enforced in courts
explanation: Inalienability means human rights cannot be taken away, waived, or transferred - they belong to every person by virtue of being human. A person cannot validly 'consent' to be enslaved or tortured. Inalienability does not mean rights are absolute - it means they cannot be permanently extinguished or given up.

question: The 'Ruggie Framework' (2011) on business and human rights establishes three pillars. Which correctly states them?
options: State duty to Protect human rights; Corporate responsibility to Respect human rights; Access to Remedy for victims
explanation: The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) - the 'Ruggie Framework' - rests on three pillars: Protect (state duty to protect against third-party human rights abuses); Respect (corporate responsibility to respect human rights - due diligence); Remedy (access to effective remedy for those affected).

question: The relationship between the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions under the PHR Act 1993 is:
options: Hierarchical - NHRC can overrule SHRC decisions
Competitive - either can take up any matter
Sequential - complaints must first go to SHRC then to NHRC
Complementary but non-hierarchical - NHRC handles central/inter-state matters, SHRC handles List II/III matters; NHRC cannot overrule SHRC
explanation: The PHR Act 1993 establishes a complementary (not hierarchical) relationship: NHRC has jurisdiction over central government and Union List matters; SHRC has jurisdiction over State and Concurrent List matters. Section 36(1) prevents NHRC from inquiring into matters pending before SHRC. NHRC cannot overrule or review SHRC decisions.

question: The 'Durban Declaration and Programme of Action' (2001) deals with:
options: Racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance
explanation: The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (DDPA) was adopted at the World Conference Against Racism (Durban, South Africa, 2001). It is the most comprehensive international document on combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance.

question: The 'right to food' as a human right in India has been recognized through:
options: Right to Food Act 2013 (National Food Security Act)
Supreme Court orders in PUCL v. UOI (2001 - ongoing) and the National Food Security Act 2013
explanation: PUCL v. UOI (2001 - 'Right to Food case') - the SC converted various food security schemes into judicially enforceable entitlements by interpreting Article 21 to include the right to food. The National Food Security Act 2013 subsequently gave statutory basis to this right.

question: The term 'stateless person' in international human rights law refers to:
options: A person who is not considered as a national by any state under the operation of its law - defined in the 1954 Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons
A refugee who has lost their nationality
A person living in a failed state
explanation: The 1954 Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons defines 'stateless person' as a person who is not considered as a national by any state under the operation of its law. Statelessness is a serious human rights problem. India is not party to either the 1954 or 1961 Convention.

question: The concept of 'positive peace' (as distinguished from 'negative peace') means:
options: A peace treaty signed with positive mutual intentions
Peace maintained by positive military force
International peace agreements that create positive legal obligations
Not merely the absence of war but the presence of justice, equality, and fulfilment of human rights
explanation: Johan Galtung (1969) distinguished: Negative peace (absence of war, direct violence) and Positive peace (absence of structural violence - presence of justice, equality, respect for human rights). This distinction is relevant to the third-generation right to peace and the development-rights nexus.

question: PIL (Public Interest Litigation) and environmental rights in India are related because:
options: PIL cannot be used for environmental matters - only regular suits can
PIL has been the primary vehicle through which environmental rights have been enforced in India, relaxing locus standi requirements
PIL is limited to fundamental rights and cannot cover environmental statutes
PIL can only be filed by registered NGOs
explanation: PIL relaxed the traditional locus standi requirement - any public-spirited citizen can approach the SC (Article 32) or HC (Article 226). This opened the floodgates for environmental litigation in India. M.C. Mehta, RLEK, Vellore Citizens, Almitra Patel - all landmark environmental cases were PILs.

question: The Principle of 'Non-Regression' in environmental law means:
options: Environmental law must always become stricter over time
State environmental standards cannot be lower than international standards
Once a certain level of environmental protection is achieved through law or policy, it should not be rolled back
Environmental regulations once enacted cannot be amended
explanation: Non-regression (or standstill principle) holds that environmental standards already achieved should not be deliberately diminished. It prevents 'regulatory rollback' - governments weakening environmental protections once achieved. Related to the prohibition on retrogression in socioeconomic rights under ICESCR.

question: UNGA Resolution 76/300 (July 2022) recognized:
options: Right to a safe climate as a human right
Right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right
Right to compensation for climate change victims
explanation: UNGA Resolution 76/300 (28 July 2022) - adopted by consensus (161 in favour, 0 against, 8 abstentions) - recognized for the first time that access to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment is a universal human right. The UNHRC had first recognized it through Resolution 48/13 (October 2021).

question: 'Climate litigation' as a global trend refers to:
options: Disputes between nations on climate finance
Lawsuits filed before domestic and international courts to compel governments and corporations to take climate action or pay for climate damage
Criminal prosecution of polluters under domestic law
explanation: Climate litigation - cases filed in domestic courts challenging government inaction on climate change. Landmark cases: Urgenda Foundation v. Netherlands (2019 - Dutch SC ordered government to reduce emissions by 25%); Neubauer v. Germany (2021 - German Constitutional Court ordered stronger climate law).

question: The 'Bharat Stage' emission norms in India are:
options: Vehicle emission standards prescribed for automobiles, modelled on European standards
Standards for thermal power plant emissions
Standards for industrial zones near urban areas
explanation: Bharat Stage (BS) emission norms are vehicular emission standards prescribed by the Central Pollution Control Board under EPA 1986. India directly leapt from BS-IV to BS-VI norms in April 2020, skipping BS-V, following directions of the Supreme Court in vehicular pollution cases.

question: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 was challenged and partially diluted by the Supreme Court in:
options: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018)
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006)
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018)
explanation: In Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018), the SC directed that: no automatic arrest on SC/ST Act complaints; prior inquiry by DSP before FIR; anticipatory bail can be granted. Parliament responded by enacting the SC/ST (POA) Amendment Act 2018 to negate this judgment.

question: The 'intersectionality' concept in human rights law (coined by Kimberle Crenshaw) means:
options: The intersection of different branches of law
The intersection of international and domestic human rights law
The way multiple forms of discrimination (race, gender, class, disability) overlap and compound each other creating unique forms of disadvantage
How human rights intersect with criminal law
explanation: Kimberle Crenshaw (1989) coined 'intersectionality' - Black women face discrimination that is not simply the sum of race discrimination + sex discrimination but is a unique, compounded form of disadvantage. This concept has been adopted in human rights law by the CEDAW Committee, CRC Committee and others.

question: The 'non-discrimination' principle in human rights law contains both 'formal equality' and 'substantive equality'. The key difference is:
options: Formal equality means identical treatment; substantive equality means treating similarly situated persons similarly
Substantive equality is more limited than formal equality
They are two names for the same concept
Formal equality means treating everyone identically regardless of circumstances; substantive equality means taking into account structural disadvantages to achieve real equality of outcomes
explanation: Formal equality (treating like cases alike) can perpetuate inequality if structural disadvantages are not addressed. Substantive equality requires positive measures to overcome historical and structural discrimination - the basis for affirmative action/reservations. Indian constitutional law through Articles 15(4), 16(4) embodies substantive equality.

question: The 'Aarhus Convention 1998' is sometimes called a bridge between:
options: Domestic law and international trade law
North and South - developed and developing nations
Environmental law and human rights law
explanation: The Aarhus Convention explicitly links environmental protection with human rights - its Preamble states that every person has the right to live in an environment adequate to their health and well-being. The three rights it protects (information, participation, access to justice) are procedural human rights applied in the environmental context.

question: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act 2015 added new offences. Which of the following was NOT an existing offence under the original 1989 Act?
options: Social or economic boycott of SC/ST communities
Forcing a member of SC/ST to leave their house or village
Committing a sexual offence against an SC/ST woman
Wrongful dispossession of land belonging to SC/ST
explanation: Social or economic boycott was not in the original SC/ST (POA) Act 1989 - it was added as a new offence by the Amendment Act 2015. The 2015 Amendment significantly expanded the list of offences to cover social boycott, garlanding with footwear, forcing to eat inedible/obnoxious substances, and other forms of social humiliation.

question: The Biological Diversity Act 2002 establishes which three-tier structure for biodiversity governance?
options: Central Board, State Board, District Board
National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards, Biodiversity Management Committees
NBA, State Forests Departments, Gram Panchayats
explanation: Biological Diversity Act 2002 establishes: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) at national level, State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) at state level, and Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at local body level. BMCs are responsible for preparing People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs).

question: Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, a person can discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream or well only with:
options: Approval of the Central Pollution Control Board
Consent of the State Pollution Control Board
Permission of the Ministry of Environment
explanation: Section 25 of the Water Act 1974: No person shall, without the previous consent of the State Board, establish or take any steps to establish any industry likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream or well. Consent of SPCB is mandatory - violation is punishable under Section 44.

question: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 empowers the State Government to declare any area as an:
explanation: Section 19 of the Air Act 1981: The State Government may, after consultation with the State Board, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare in such manner as may be prescribed, any area or areas within the State as air pollution control area. Once declared, no person can use any fuel other than approved fuel.

question: The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016 replaced which earlier rules?
options: Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2008
explanation: The Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 replaced the Hazardous Wastes Rules 2008. The 2016 Rules introduced a new category called 'other wastes' (like paper waste, metal scrap) separate from hazardous wastes and streamlined procedures for transboundary movement.

question: The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017 were framed under:
explanation: Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017 replaced the Wetlands Rules 2010 and were framed under EPA 1986. They prohibit certain activities in wetlands (industrialization, solid waste dumping, construction) and provide for Wetland Authorities at state level.

question: The Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 were enacted to implement:
explanation: ODS Rules 2000 (framed under EPA 1986) implement India's obligations under the Montreal Protocol 1987 by regulating production, import, export, sale and use of ozone-depleting substances including CFCs, HCFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride and methyl bromide.

question: The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 introduced the concept of:
options: Community reserves as a new protected area category
Conservation reserves - to connect protected areas
explanation: Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 introduced: regulation of invasive alien species (IAS) for the first time in Indian wildlife law; simplified protected area management; reduced schedules from 6 to 4; brought CITES implementation under the Act; and strengthened provisions on captive animals and zoos.

question: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) in India are prescribed by:
options: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Central Pollution Control Board under the Air Act 1981
explanation: National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) are prescribed by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981. The current NAAQS were revised in 2009. They set permissible concentration limits for 12 pollutants including PM10, PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO, Ozone, Lead.

question: The 'Polluter Pays Principle' as applied to ship-source marine pollution is primarily embodied in:
options: International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage (CLC) 1969 and Fund Convention
explanation: The Civil Liability Convention (CLC) 1969 (and its 1992 Protocol) imposes strict liability on shipowners for oil pollution damage from tankers and requires compulsory insurance. The International Oil Pollution Compensation (IOPC) Fund provides additional compensation - implementing Polluter Pays Principle in the maritime context.

question: The Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Agreement (2023) deals with:
options: Conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction (high seas)
Biodiversity conservation in Antarctic regions only
explanation: The BBNJ Agreement (also called the 'High Seas Treaty') was adopted in June 2023 under UNCLOS. It is the first international treaty to protect marine biodiversity in the high seas (beyond national jurisdiction, covering 64% of the ocean). It covers marine genetic resources, area-based management tools, EIA in high seas.

question: The 'equitable utilization' principle in international water law means:
options: Each riparian state is entitled to a reasonable and equitable share of the waters of an international watercourse, considering all relevant factors
All riparian states get equal shares of shared rivers
Upstream states have priority over downstream states
Water resources are distributed based on population
explanation: The principle of equitable utilization is the cornerstone of international water law, codified in the UN Convention on the Law of Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses 1997. No single factor determines 'equitable' share - relevant factors include geographic position, climate, past utilization, population needs, and conservation measures.

question: The 'non-binding' nature of the Rio Declaration 1992 means:
options: It does not create binding treaty obligations but its principles have been widely recognized as reflecting or contributing to customary international environmental law
Its principles have no relevance in international or domestic law
States can completely ignore the Declaration
Only states that voted for it are bound by it
explanation: The Rio Declaration is soft law - not a binding treaty. However, its 27 principles have significantly influenced international environmental law: several have been recognized as reflecting customary international law, incorporated into binding treaties, and applied by domestic courts including Indian courts in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum 1996.

question: The 'Kigali Amendment' to the Montreal Protocol (2016) deals with:
options: Phasing down hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) which are potent greenhouse gases used as substitutes for CFCs
Extending the Protocol to developing countries
Creating a new fund for ozone layer restoration
explanation: The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol requires parties to phase down production and consumption of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). While HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer, they are powerful greenhouse gases. The Amendment is expected to prevent up to 0.5 degrees C of global warming by 2100. India ratified it in 2021.

question: The Supreme Court in S. Jagannath v. Union of India (1997) - the Shrimp Culture case - applied which principle?
options: Public Trust Doctrine to privatize beaches
Precautionary principle and Polluter Pays principle to order closure of shrimp farms in coastal ecologically sensitive areas
Sustainable development to permit shrimp farming with conditions
explanation: S. Jagannath v. UOI (1997) - Shrimp Culture case: The SC applied the Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle to order closure of shrimp (prawn) farms within 500 metres of the High Tide Line in coastal states, holding they were causing irreversible damage to mangroves and coastal ecology.

question: Under the Forest Rights Act 2006, the authority empowered to receive, verify and approve/reject forest rights claims is:
options: Three-tier structure - Gram Sabha (initial recognition), Sub-Divisional Level Committee, District Level Committee
explanation: Forest Rights Act 2006 provides a three-tier adjudication: Gram Sabha (initiates the process, receives claims, prepares maps); Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC - examines and forwards); District Level Committee (DLC - final authority to approve or reject). The Gram Sabha is the entry point for all claims.

question: The 'Doctrine of Parens Patriae' has been applied in environmental law in India to mean:
options: The State as guardian of the environment and natural resources on behalf of the public
Parents' right to a clean environment for their children
A doctrine imposing personal liability on company directors for environmental damage
Power of the court to appoint environmental commissioners
explanation: Parens patriae (parent of the nation) - in environmental law, Indian courts have used it to hold that the State is the guardian/trustee of natural resources on behalf of the public (linked to the Public Trust Doctrine). Courts can direct the State to perform its parens patriae duties when it fails to protect environmental resources.

question: The 'National Action Plan on Climate Change' (NAPCC) was launched in India in:
explanation: India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) was launched in June 2008. It has eight national missions including: National Solar Mission; National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency; National Water Mission; National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem; National Mission for a Green India; National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture.

question: The 'Four Freedoms' speech by President Franklin D. Roosevelt (1941) articulated:
options: Freedom of speech, freedom of press, freedom of assembly, freedom of petition
Freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom from want, freedom from fear
Life, liberty, property and pursuit of happiness
explanation: FDR's Four Freedoms (January 1941 State of the Union address): Freedom of speech and expression; Freedom of worship (religion); Freedom from want (economic security); Freedom from fear (global reduction of armaments). These articulations directly influenced the drafting of the UN Charter and UDHR.

question: The 'Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples' (UN General Assembly Resolution 1514, 1960) recognized:
options: Right of all peoples to self-determination and immediate independence from colonialism
Right to participate in democratic elections
Rights of minority communities within colonies
explanation: UNGA Resolution 1514 (XV) 1960: proclaimed that all peoples have the right to self-determination and that alien subjugation, domination and exploitation constitute a denial of fundamental human rights. It accelerated the decolonization process and established self-determination as a binding norm.

question: The 'International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination' (ICERD) was adopted in:
explanation: ICERD was adopted by UNGA on 21 December 1965 and entered into force in 1969. It is the first of the core UN human rights treaties to be adopted after the UDHR. The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) monitors its implementation. India ratified ICERD in 1968.

question: The 'Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment' (CAT) was adopted in:
explanation: CAT (Convention Against Torture) was adopted by UNGA on 10 December 1984 and entered into force in 1987. It defines torture, prohibits it absolutely, and requires criminalization, universal jurisdiction, non-refoulement in torture cases, and the right to rehabilitation for victims. India signed in 1997 but has NOT ratified CAT.

question: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Persons Belonging to National or Ethnic, Religious and Linguistic Minorities was adopted in:
explanation: UNGA Resolution 47/135 adopted the Declaration on Minorities on 18 December 1992. It builds on ICCPR Article 27 and provides more detailed protection - states shall protect the existence and national/ethnic/cultural/religious/linguistic identity of minorities and adopt measures to that end.

question: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 declares a child marriage:
options: Void ab initio in all cases
A criminal offence but valid marriage
Voidable at the option of the contracting party who was a child at the time of marriage
Void only if solemnized under Hindu personal law
explanation: Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006: A child marriage is voidable (not void ab initio) at the option of the party who was a child - the child can file a petition for annulment before the District Court within two years of attaining majority. Certain child marriages can be declared void when the minor is taken by fraud, force, or allurement.

question: The Domestic Violence Act 2005 defines 'domestic relationship' to include:
options: Only husband and wife in a legally registered marriage
Persons who live or have lived together in a shared household - including marriage, relationship in nature of marriage, family, and adoption
Only persons related by marriage under personal laws
explanation: Section 2(f) of the DV Act 2005 defines 'domestic relationship' broadly: a relationship between two persons who live or have lived together at any point in time in a shared household, when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption, or are family members living as a joint family.

question: The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act 1994 was enacted to:
options: Regulate prenatal care for pregnant women
Prevent birth of children with genetic disorders
Prohibit sex determination of foetus before or after conception and prevent female foeticide
explanation: PCPNDT Act 1994 prohibits: use of any technique for sex determination before or after conception; advertisement of such techniques; sex-selective abortion. It mandates registration of all ultrasound clinics and genetic counselling centres. The Act was amended in 2003 to cover pre-conception techniques.

question: The NHRC can, under Section 18 of the PHR Act 1993, approach the Supreme Court or High Court for:
options: Issuing binding directions to the government
Seeking directions or orders where it considers it necessary to do so for enforcement of its recommendations
Filing criminal complaints against human rights violators
Seeking enhancement of its powers beyond the Act
explanation: Section 18(b) of PHR Act 1993: If the Commission considers it necessary, it may approach the Supreme Court or the concerned High Court for the issue of such directions, orders or writs as that Court may deem necessary. This gives the NHRC a route to convert its non-binding recommendations into court-enforceable orders.

question: The National Commission for Minorities Act 1992 defines 'minority' to mean:
options: Any community that forms less than 50% of the national population
A community notified as a minority by the Central Government
Religious minorities only as defined by the Constitution
explanation: The NCM Act 1992 does not define 'minority' by any fixed criterion - Section 2(c) defines 'minority' as a community notified as such by the Central Government. This is why the power to notify minorities is entirely with the Central Government.

question: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes under Article 338 submits its annual report to:
options: The President of India who causes it to be laid before Parliament along with a memorandum of action taken
The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
explanation: Article 338(5) and (6): The NCSC shall present annually to the President a report on the working of its safeguards. The President shall cause all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament, together with a memorandum explaining action taken or proposed to be taken on the recommendations.

question: The term of office of the Chairperson and Members of the NHRC under the PHR Act 1993 (as amended in 2019) is:
options: 5 years or age of 75 years, whichever is earlier
3 years or age of 70 years, whichever is earlier
At the pleasure of the President
explanation: PHR Act 1993 as amended in 2019: The Chairperson and every Member shall hold office for a term of three years from the date on which they enter upon their office or until they attain the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier. They are not eligible for reappointment. Previously the term was 5 years.

question: Which of the following statements about the NHRC is CORRECT?
options: NHRC can suo motu initiate inquiry only if a court directs it to do so
NHRC has both civil and criminal jurisdiction
NHRC can visit and inspect jails and other places of detention under intimation to state government
NHRC can inquire into violations committed more than 2 years before the complaint
explanation: Section 12(c) and Section 14 of PHR Act 1993: The NHRC may visit, under intimation to the State Government, any institution under the control of the State Government where persons are detained or lodged for purposes of treatment, reformation or protection. The words 'under intimation' means it informs but need not seek prior permission.

question: Who is known as the 'Father of International Environmental Law'?
explanation: Maurice Strong (Canadian diplomat) is widely regarded as the Father of International Environmental Law. He was the Secretary-General of both the Stockholm Conference 1972 and the Rio Earth Summit 1992. He also served as the first Executive Director of UNEP.

question: Who chaired the Brundtland Commission that produced the report 'Our Common Future' (1987)?
explanation: Gro Harlem Brundtland - former Prime Minister of Norway and later Director-General of WHO - chaired the World Commission on Environment and Development (1983-1987). The Commission's report 'Our Common Future' gave the most widely cited definition of sustainable development.

question: The lawyer who filed the maximum number of landmark environmental PILs in India's Supreme Court is:
explanation: M.C. Mehta (Mahesh Chandra Mehta) is an Indian environmental lawyer who filed the largest number of landmark environmental PILs in the Supreme Court - the Ganga pollution case, Oleum gas case, Taj Trapezium case, vehicular pollution case etc. He received the Goldman Environmental Prize in 1996 and Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1997.

question: The Chipko Movement (1973) in India was associated with which personalities?
options: Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt
explanation: The Chipko Movement (1973, Uttarakhand) - women hugging trees to prevent felling - was associated with Chandi Prasad Bhatt (who organized the movement in Gopeshwar) and Sunderlal Bahuguna (who gave it national prominence through his padyatras). 'Chipko' means to embrace/hug.

question: The Narmada Bachao Andolan against the Sardar Sarovar Dam is associated with:
explanation: Medha Patkar is the founder and leader of the Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA) - the movement against the Sardar Sarovar Dam on River Narmada, raising issues of displacement of tribal and rural communities, lack of rehabilitation, and submergence of forest and agricultural land.

question: 'Silent Spring' (1962) - the book credited with launching the modern environmental movement globally - was written by:
explanation: Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' (1962) documented the harmful effects of pesticides (especially DDT) on the environment, particularly birds. It led to the ban on DDT in the USA in 1972 and is credited with launching the modern environmental movement, inspiring the first Earth Day (1970).

question: The concept of 'intergenerational equity' in environmental law was developed by:
explanation: Edith Brown Weiss (Georgetown University) developed the concept of intergenerational equity in her book 'In Fairness to Future Generations: International Law, Common Patrimony and Intergenerational Equity' (1989). She proposed three principles: conservation of options, conservation of quality, and conservation of access.

question: Eleanor Roosevelt described the UDHR as:
options: 'An international Magna Carta for all mankind'
'A beacon of hope for all nations'
explanation: Eleanor Roosevelt described the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as 'an international Magna Carta for all mankind' - drawing a parallel with the Magna Carta 1215 as a foundational document limiting arbitrary power.

question: The Indian delegate to the UN Commission on Human Rights who ensured that UDHR Article 1 reads 'all human beings' instead of 'all men' was:
explanation: Hansa Mehta - Indian delegate - successfully argued that Article 1 of the UDHR should read 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights' instead of the original 'All men are born free...' This change gave the UDHR its explicitly gender-neutral and inclusive character.

question: Rene Cassin - who won the Nobel Peace Prize 1968 - is associated with:
options: Drafting the European Convention on Human Rights
Establishing the International Court of Justice
Being the principal drafter of the UDHR
explanation: Rene Cassin (French jurist and judge) was the principal drafter of the UDHR and played a central role in the UN Commission on Human Rights under Eleanor Roosevelt's chairmanship. He later served as President of the European Court of Human Rights. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1968.

question: The term 'genocide' was coined by:
explanation: Raphael Lemkin (Polish-Jewish lawyer) coined the term 'genocide' in his book 'Axis Rule in Occupied Europe' (1944) - combining the Greek word 'genos' (race/people) and the Latin suffix '-cide' (killing). He campaigned for the Genocide Convention 1948, adopted one day before the UDHR.

question: The 'Three Pillars of Sustainable Development' as articulated at the World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, 2002) are:
options: Economic development, Social development, Environmental protection
explanation: The Johannesburg Declaration (2002) reaffirmed the three pillars of sustainable development: Economic development, Social development, and Environmental protection. These three pillars are interdependent and mutually reinforcing.

question: 'Small is Beautiful' (1973) - an influential book on economics and environment - was written by:
explanation: E.F. Schumacher's 'Small is Beautiful: Economics As If People Mattered' (1973) argued against the obsession with GDP growth and large-scale industrialization, advocating for human-scale, sustainable economic systems. It influenced the concept of appropriate technology and sustainable development discourse.

question: The first Executive Director of UNEP was:
explanation: Maurice Strong served as the first Executive Director of UNEP when it was established in 1972 following the Stockholm Conference. He served until 1975. The UNEP headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya - the only UN body headquartered in a developing country.

question: Vandana Shiva - physicist turned environmental activist - is known for work on:
options: Biodiversity, biopiracy, organic farming, and the rights of farmers - seed sovereignty
explanation: Vandana Shiva is known for her work on biodiversity, biopiracy, organic farming, and the rights of farmers (seed sovereignty). She founded the Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology. She is particularly associated with the Chipko movement connections and work on seed sovereignty.

question: The first Earth Day was observed on:
explanation: The first Earth Day was observed on 22 April 1970 in the United States, organized by Senator Gaylord Nelson. It mobilized 20 million Americans and led to the creation of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the enactment of the US Clean Air Act. April 22 is now observed as Earth Day globally.

question: World Environment Day is observed every year on:
explanation: World Environment Day is observed every year on 5 June - the date on which the Stockholm Conference on Human Environment opened in 1972. It was established by UNGA in 1972 and is the UN's principal vehicle for encouraging awareness and action for protection of the environment.

question: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities is observed on:
explanation: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities is observed on 3 December every year, established by UNGA Resolution 47/3 (1992). It promotes an understanding of disability issues and mobilizes support for the dignity, rights and well-being of persons with disabilities.

question: Human Rights Day is observed on:
explanation: Human Rights Day is observed every year on 10 December - the date on which the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. It is one of the most widely observed international days worldwide.

question: The UDHR has how many articles in total?
explanation: The UDHR has 30 articles covering: Articles 1-2 (foundational principles of dignity and non-discrimination); Articles 3-21 (civil and political rights); Articles 22-27 (economic, social and cultural rights); Articles 28-30 (collective rights and duties).

question: The Convention on the Rights of the Child has how many articles?
explanation: The CRC has 54 articles divided into three parts: Part I (Articles 1-41) - substantive rights; Part II (Articles 42-45) - implementation and monitoring; Part III (Articles 46-54) - final clauses on ratification, entry into force etc. This number (54) is a frequently tested fact.

question: The ICCPR was opened for signature in which year?
explanation: The ICCPR was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 16 December 1966 (the same day as the ICESCR) and opened for signature. It entered into force on 23 March 1976 after receiving the required 35 ratifications. India ratified the ICCPR on 10 April 1979.

question: The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 received Presidential assent on:
explanation: The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 received the assent of the President on 8 January 1994. However, the NHRC was actually constituted earlier on 12 October 1993 through an ordinance/notification. Both dates are testable - know the distinction.

question: The NGT has how many zonal benches apart from the Principal Bench?
explanation: The NGT has 4 zonal benches apart from the Principal Bench at New Delhi: Central Zone bench at Bhopal; Western Zone bench at Pune; Eastern Zone bench at Kolkata; Southern Zone bench at Chennai. Total = 1 Principal Bench + 4 Zonal Benches = 5 locations.

question: The Ozone Layer is found in which layer of the Earth's atmosphere?
explanation: The ozone layer (ozone-sphere) is located in the stratosphere, approximately 15-35 km above the Earth's surface. It absorbs 97-99% of the Sun's medium-frequency ultraviolet light. Depletion of the ozone layer leads to increased UV-B radiation causing skin cancer, cataracts, and damage to marine ecosystems.

question: The Montreal Protocol has been ratified by how many countries - making it:
options: The first UN treaty to achieve universal ratification (197 parties)
explanation: The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer is the first - and so far only - UN treaty to achieve universal ratification, with all 197 UN member states as parties. This is why it is considered the most successful multilateral environmental agreement in history.

question: The number of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted in 2015 is:
explanation: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development has 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets. The 17 SDGs replaced the 8 Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). Key SDGs: SDG 6 (clean water), SDG 13 (climate action), SDG 14 (oceans), SDG 15 (life on land), SDG 16 (peace, justice, institutions).

question: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in which year and entered into force in which year?
explanation: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997 at COP3 in Kyoto, Japan. It entered into force on 16 February 2005 after Russia's ratification. India ratified in 2002. The 8-year gap between adoption and entry into force is a testable detail.

question: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 on which date?
